desc:
Encoding. A singly linked list is passed to your function as an array holding the node values from head to tail; an empty array is an empty list. You may build real nodes from it first, or work on the array directly. The result is also returned as an array of values from head to tail.

Rotate the list to the right by k places: one rotation step moves the last node to the front. Return the values after k steps.

For example [1,2,3,4,5] with k = 2 gives [4,5,1,2,3]. Note that k can be far larger than the length of the list, so doing the steps one by one is too slow.
hints: After n rotations (n = length) the list is back to the start, so only k mod n matters. Watch out for the empty list.
Rotating right by r means the last r nodes move to the front. Which node becomes the new tail?

Find the length and the tail node, make the list circular by linking tail to head, then walk n - r steps from the head. The node you stop on is the new tail; its successor is the new head. Cut the circle there.
editorial: Compute the length n in one pass while remembering the tail. Reduce k to r = k mod n; when r is 0 (or the list is empty) nothing changes. Otherwise the new tail is the node at index n - r - 1 (0-based) and the new head is the node right after it.

Link the old tail to the old head to close the ring, advance n - r - 1 steps from the head to the new tail, take its next as the new head and set its next to null. The total work is O(n) and O(1) extra space, independent of how large k is.
